hypothesis: Predict replies from an opponent that knows our own Flag and Spy, while preserving our uncertainty about every concealed enemy identity.
recommendation: Keep this experiment limited to the original DOS initial Flag/Spy grant. It is a clear, independently evidenced information-model change.
honesty: Our player already knows its own Flag and Spy positions. Supplying those facts to a hypothetical opponent model grants our player no concealed enemy information. The real enemy setup remains absent from its transport and observer.

historical_view_audit.checked: All initial and current decision boards reconstructed from sampled worlds and public trajectories. Only the simulated opponent receives additional root-owned Flag/Spy identities. Real enemy ranks remain masked to root policies.

why_not_add_conditional_rank_access_now: The initial Flag/Spy grant is a fixed, directly tested property. Later original-engine rank accesses are conditional and need their own trigger and availability model.
Giving every root-owned rank to every simulated opponent would be a full-information stress model, not an accurate reproduction of those conditional paths.
Combining grants would prevent a clean attribution of any measured change to the initial Flag/Spy information.
If later access is investigated, instrument and specify it separately, register a new immutable policy and use new validation seeds.
interpretation_limits: The simulated opponent still uses the project's native student policy, not the original DOS move-selection code. Matching information alone does not make it a calibrated DOS opponent model.
The root continuation policy itself is held fixed. Counterstrategy enters through changed predicted opponent replies and root action evaluation.
Positive DOS results would support this inexpensive opponent-information correction. Negative results would not establish that knowledge-aware opponent modelling cannot help.
